Six clear modes are detected, which come from oscillations of the free layer (labeled F0, F1, ...) and the SAF structure (A0, A1, and A2). The free layer modes are V-shaped, while the modes not showing a minimum at low fields correspond to SAF modes (Helmer et al., 2010). The analysis of the F0 and F1 modes was carried out in the manner discussed in Ref. Houssameddine et al. (2008). The analysis of these results reveals that for negative currents, a decrease in frequency is observed for the first and second modes in the P state, starting at J ∼ -10 7 A/cm 2 . The change of the oscillation frequency with respect to the TFMR regime and the linewidth of the F0 and F1 modes for the P ( H =-350 Oe) and AP (250 Oe) states is shown in Fig. 7.8a,b, resembling the transition from T-FMR to SSP reported on similar devices in Ref. Houssameddine et al. (2008).

The minimum linewidth /Delta1 f obtained for the F0 mode is around 400 MHz, concluding that the highest negative current takes the sample to an intermittent SSP regime (Houssameddine et al., 2009). The AP state, however, presents no signs of such a transition, and the frequency of the modes in Fig. 7.8a remains constant with the current.

Figures 4(a) and 4(b) illustrate the Raman spectra and the associated intensity color plot when the incident light is falling on the m plane. A distinct periodic variation in intensity of the Raman modes [Figs. 4(c)-4(f)] has been observed with respect to the angular rotation. The contrasting behavior of the E g and A 1g modes indicates the anisotropic interactions of light with Bi2Te3 crystals in the m plane. A similar pattern has been observed for ∼ 633 nm excitation (Supplemental Material Fig. S3 [27]), confirming the intrinsic nature of structurally driven (an/)isotropic light-matter interactions in these materials. The mode frequency as well as full width at half maximum for 532 nm, with respect to the angle of polarized light, shows negligible variation as shown in Supplemental Material Fig. S4 [27].
